paper_title: HandsOn: A Large-Scale Simulation Benchmark for Generalizable Dexterous Manipulation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: General-purpose manipulation requires reliable behavior across embodiments, objects, and task demands. We introduce HandsOn, a composable simulation platform and benchmark for cross-embodiment dexterous manipulation. It supports five robotic arms, six dexterous hands, and approximately 200 rigid, articulated, and deformable assets in randomized scenes. The benchmark pairs 18,000 curated human demonstrations with 66 human-verified tasks: Core-50 supports demonstration-based learning and execution tests, while Transfer-16 evaluates asset and relation transfer, skill composition, and deformable manipulation without target-task training demonstrations. Qualitative real-robot rollouts illustrate sim-to-real transfer. Across diffusion, vision-language-action, world-action, and prompted VLM-based methods, the best trained multi-task policy achieves 29.1% Core-50 success. Without benchmark finetuning, GPT-6 using move_eef for palm-and-finger control achieves 5.2% on Core-50 and 1.9% on Transfer-16 over 660 trials. Trained-policy stage diagnostics expose failures in contact establishment, action coordination, and maintaining achieved goals, with additional sequencing errors in composed tasks. HandsOn provides a shared basis for investigating manipulation generalization and the limits of reliable physical interaction.

Introduction Dexterous manipulation requires controlling how contacts change during an operation. Moving mouse must not trigger premature click; setting two knobs requires both knobs to remain at their target settings simultaneously; and placing lid requires preserving alignment while releasing it. Evaluating these capabilities requires demonstrations of varied interactions and diagnostics that distinguish initial progress from reliable functional completion. Recent dexterous benchmarks broaden task and embodiment coverage [14], but their human-demonstration sets are small and their tasks rarely include ones reserved for evaluation. HandsOn provides 18,000 curated simulation demonstrations, approximately 56 hours of interaction with three synchronized camera views. This is 5.716.4 times the human trajectory count of representative dexterous benchmarks under the convention in Table 1. High-fidelity re-rendering produces varied observations of recorded behavior while preserving state/action supervision. Visual domain randomization and meaning-preserving prompt randomization broaden appearance and language coverage around task-specific configurations. Figure 1 summarizes the asset collection, environment and interaction diversity, demonstration scale, and Core-50 results. Figure 2 connects this data pipeline to evaluation and illustrates correspondence with the physical system. Figure 2 Platform and evaluation protocol. (a) Toy-aircraft views: setup (not policy input), wrist (W), and main (M). Real images show appearance; real rollouts are qualitative videos. (b) Nine trained methods and GPT-6 (move_eef); GPT-6 uses no HandsOn training. (c) Separate suite-specific counts and results. (d) Trained-policy failures (Section 5.3.3). 4 HandsOn: Generalizable Dexterous Manipulation The benchmark comprises two complementary suites: Core-50, 50 tasks with demonstrations for policy learning and fresh-rollout evaluation, and Transfer-16, 16 tasks reserved for generalization evaluation. Core-50 tasks combine functional and numerical understanding, articulation, spatial relations, precise contacts, and bimanual execution (Figure 3). Transfer-16 tests new asset relations and skill combinations, including three deformable interactions without deformable-task demonstrations in this dataset. The simulated embodiment follows physical platform, and real-robot rollouts of simulation-trained checkpoints are shown in the accompanying videos. Our Core-50 study compares ten methods: five VLA models, three WAM models, single-task Diffusion Policy, and the prompted VLM controller GPT-6. The best trained multi-task score is 29.1%. Across the trained checkpoints, tool use and precision fits are nearly unsolved, and skill-group gaps persist after adjusting for demonstration count and expert duration. Two VLA checkpoints barely condition on which object the instruction names. Failures concentrate where closing the grasp fires button, where both hands must hold their targets together, and where reached goals must be kept. These findings motivate evaluating what happens after acquisition, alongside aggregate success. We additionally study GPT-6 as prompted multimodal controller, using RGB observations, measured robot state, and the move_eef palm-and-finger control interface without HandsOn finetuning. This supplementary experiment achieves 5.2% success on Core-50 and 1.9% on Transfer-16 over 660 trials. Success appears on only 12 of the 66 tasks. Qualitative action traces suggest task-level planning potential and motivate richer interfaces between that planning and high-dimensional dexterous execution. Its observation interface, trial count, and model-call budgets are disclosed alongside the trained-policy comparison. The HandsOn Benchmark HandsOn has two suites. Core-50 provides demonstrations for policy learning and fresh-rollout evaluation; Transfer-16 is reserved for generalization evaluation and contributes no target-task demonstration to the training set. Both suites are scored by native, task-specific success predicates rather than by shared proxy, and every task was verified in person by the data-collection operators before release (Section 3.2). 3.1. Core-50 and Transfer-16 Core-50 tasks combine functional and numerical understanding, articulation, spatial relations, precise contacts, and bimanual execution (Figure 3). Transfer-16 tests new asset relations and skill compositions, including three deformable interactions for which this dataset contains no deformabletask demonstrations. Because the two suites answer different questions, we report them separately throughout: Core-50 score measures execution on tasks with demonstrations, whereas Transfer-16 tests held-out tasks. Task Design and Feasibility Verification Tasks and demonstrations pass written collection-and-review procedure with separated roles: datacollection operators record and self-check episodes, independent reviewers judge them, and third person arbitrates disagreements; nobody reviews their own data. Each task has task card that fixes the goal, the standard initial and final states, completion evidence independent of the programs success flag (object poses, joint states, or images), allowed and forbidden actions with known shortcuts, the time limit, and the environment, task, and checker versions with their code hashes. new task or major revision is first piloted with at least 20 operator episodes, all reviewed by hand and covering success, failure, time-out, reset, and boundary states; it enters collection only with no severe defect, at least 98% agreement between labels and the objective evidence, and unambiguous rules. During collection the environment and checker are frozen by hash. checker change passes reproduction, impact analysis, two-person review, regression tests on normal, failing, boundary, and known-defect cases, and new fully reviewed pilot; affected episodes are replayed, relabeled, or quarantined. Every recorded episode then passes automatic checks of completeness, version hashes, action plausibility, agreement between the success flag and the final physical state, and duplication. Stratified random blind review covers about 20% of each batch (all of the first batch of new task or version), and further 510% of passed episodes are blindly re-reviewed. success flag without objective completion quarantines the task as suspected checker defect until it is repaired and piloted again. This procedure matters for how the results should be read. Every Core-50 and Transfer-16 task was verified in person by the data-collection operators in the released environment before evaluation. Each Core-50 task is also completed by its curated demonstrations. For 47 of the 50 Core-50 tasks, at least one evaluated multi-task checkpoint succeeds in at least one episode. Stopping and success. After every executed action the native environment checks success, taskdefined failure, and timeout. The rollout stops at the first terminal outcome, including within an action chunk; unused predicted actions are discarded. Diagnostics and Statistical Reporting Success and failure alone do not say where policy stops working. We record native-stage diagnostics where supported by the task checker and report their coverage explicitly. Task success and ordered progress. Primary scores are per-task success and macro-averages over declared task sets. Native executable success predicates and physical-duration holds determine completion. For task with 𝐾𝑖 stages, ordered progress is 𝑃𝑒 = 𝐿𝑒/𝐾𝑖, where 𝐿𝑒 is the longest valid ordered prefix completed in episode 𝑒. Stages are defined by semantic operations; merely approaching or touching an object does not complete functional stage. Progress never overrides the final success predicate. Ordered progress is reported for the trained multi-task methods; GPT-6 has no graded-progress measurement. Capability-specific diagnostics. Functional completion separates acquiring tool from operating it. Stability measures include drops, slip, and displacement of an object supported by the other hand when these quantities are observable. Deformable tasks additionally report task-specific geometric progress. Contact-force measures require validated sensors or simulator measurements; command magnitude is never treated as measured force. We distinguish tool acquisition from functional activation, requested numeric setting from any actuator movement, and articulated travel from mere object contact. Capability labels overlap and use disclosed membership; their averages are not added into new overall score. 9 HandsOn: Generalizable Dexterous Manipulation Figure 4 Human demonstration collection. Gloves record finger articulation and wrist trackers record hand motion. Retargeted commands drive the simulated armhand system while the operator observes the scene. Trials and uncertainty. Trials preserve task-local resets, assets, source/goal weights, state/action semantics, and checkpoint-owned preprocessing and normalization. Independent evaluation seeds are shared across compatible model comparisons. Binary success receives Wilson intervals; aggregate uncertainty is reported with the resampling unit specified. Missing or environment-invalid trials are not numerical policy failures. Every aggregate identifies its task and trial coverage, and checkpoint selection, benchmark-development exposure, and historical data exposure are disclosed in the run record. Reading the diagnostics. Native event-arrival rates and ordered completion scores are different quantities. conditional transition rate requires joint, order-consistent events, not division of unrelated stage marginals. Retention diagnostics identify both the achieved condition and the subsequent observation interval; success-triggered termination can give episodes unequal exposure. Recorded action commands are not measured wrist motion or contact force. 4. The HandsOn Data Platform HandsOn pairs teleoperated demonstration corpus with re-rendering pipeline. Collection produces exact state and action supervision at the cost of fixed set of recorded appearances; re-rendering then varies the observations around that recorded behaviour while the interaction and its labels stay fixed. The two halves are described in turn. 4.1. Collection System and Operators Demonstrations are collected in NVIDIA Isaac Sim 5.1 [25]. MANUS Prime gloves capture finger articulation, and wrist-mounted HTC VIVE Trackers provide global wrist poses [26, 27]. After frame registration and temporal alignment, wrist motion and palm-centred 21-keypoint hand representation are converted to commands. The arm branch produces feasible end-effector targets through robot kinematics; Wuji retargeting maps hand keypoints to joint targets, with 20 outputs for the first-generation Wuji Hand [28]. Simulation records synchronized observations, measured state, commanded actions, language, and source metadata (Figure 4). At least ten operators contributed over 1,050 collection sessions, which is why the feasibility procedure of Section 3.2 separates recording from review. All demonstrations are simulated: no physical robot recordings enter the training set, and the physical platform of Section 4.5 is used only for the qualitative rollouts of Appendix F. 10 HandsOn: Generalizable Dexterous Manipulation 4.2. Dataset Composition and Identity The released dataset contains 18,000 curated trajectories: 15,178 training and 2,822 validation. Selection uses task-group quotas of 500, 300, or 100 trajectories, favouring shorter eligible demonstrations within each quota. This is curated distribution, not an unbiased sample of all collected behaviour. Three stages of one multi-stage source task share quota, giving 52 quota groups. Three simultaneous camera views do not multiply the interaction duration. Across the package the median trajectory has 262 steps (10th90th percentile 96705); per Core-50 task, training trajectories range from 46 to 463 (median 268) and expert P75 durations from 2.5 to 49.2 (median 12.7 s). Split membership is defined at trajectory or session level and re-rendered derivatives inherit it; normalization fitted for this package uses training data only, and checkpoint that inherits another normalization or has historical exposure retains that provenance. High-Fidelity Re-rendering Re-rendering varies appearance while replaying the recorded interaction. Final-package capture records use 32 samples per pixel; higher-sampling presentation renders are identified separately. The implemented bank includes four table materials, three background configurations, and three ceiling styles, with texture scale and orientation, surface roughness and tint, and illumination direction, intensity, and colour-temperature variations. One verified source camera configuration samples each camera once per trajectory within 2 mm translation and 0.3 rotation per axis, retaining intrinsics. Episode records identify source trajectory and runtime, render revision, appearance seed and configuration, and camera configuration. Appearance is sampled per trajectory and remains fixed during replay; independently resampling appearance every frame is outside this static-domain protocol, and any temporal sensor noise would require separate model. Not every factor can be varied by replay alone. Table 4 states what each factor must preserve. Background and appearance changes can be applied during replay because the recorded actions remain valid; geometry and dynamics changes alter the reachable interaction and require valid re-execution rather than frozen-state replay. We use the taxonomy of Table 4 as the rule for adding variation: factor is admitted only with the evidence its row requires. 11 HandsOn: Generalizable Dexterous Manipulation Camera perturbations are composed with task-specific nominal calibration. Within the trainedcheckpoint Core-50 evaluation, which of the four table materials, three colour palettes, or two roughness levels is drawn does not measurably change success (Section 5.3.4). Those factors lie inside the training distribution, so this is an invariance check rather than visual-generalization result. 4.4. Language Bank and Prompt Sampling The frozen language bank contains 108 taskinstruction entries, of which 91 occur in the final 18,000-trajectory manifest. For these 91 active entries, there are 32 training and eight held-out paraphrases per entry, yielding 2,912 training and 728 held-out paraphrases. For example, Pick the apple and place it into the bucket and Grab the apple and put it in the bucket preserve the same goal. Replacing apple with banana, changing knob angle, or changing operation order instead requires an episode with the corresponding executable goal, which is why those variations are task variations rather than paraphrases. Held-out strings have no exact overlap with any active canonical or training string; this is lexical disjointness check, and semantic equivalence additionally requires preserving the episodes target and constraints. Inactive bank entries are not counted as demonstrated goals. The packaged sampler hashes the language seed, epoch, episode identity, frame index, draw index, and split to choose an instruction, and offers training, canonical, and unseen modes. The reference training mixture is 20% canonical and 80% training paraphrases; fixed validation uses the runs declared language mode. Language sampling does not resample the scene, cameras, or physics. model record must identify the language bank revision, the actual sampling policy, prompt preprocessing, and whether conditioning is text, structured goal, or fixed task identifier. Section 5.3.2 examines whether policies condition their actions on the object specified in the instruction. 4.5. The simulated kinematics, asset scale, cameras, state and action frames, and timing follow this physical system, and the correspondence record is given in Appendix B.1. 4.6. Line Up Blocks, Scoop Marbles, and Flip Sponge end on direct hand contact with the manipulated object in 81, 44, and 28% of episodes (2 successes in 2,400): policies pursue the object with the hand rather than through the tool. On the 41 fixed-goal tasks at least one checkpoint solves 62.4% of scenes, close to the 64.0% expected under independence (median pairwise 𝜅 = 0.03): the failed scenes differ by checkpoint, so no shared set of hard scenes explains the failures, although each checkpoint may have its own. Transfer-16 fails at the same transitions, and new objects fail earlier. Every matched transition fails more often than in its Core-50 source (Figure 8c). In Spray Shoe grasps form in 232 of 344 episodes, but at most 3 of 43 per checkpoint complete trigger cycle. On solved source, new object moves failure to acquisition: the left hand picks up the glue stick in 5 of 400 Pass Glue Stick episodes, against 4088% per checkpoint in Pass Block. Compositions add fourth failure: steps are repeated or started early. After the laptop step (146 episodes), no episode brings the mouse onto its pad, and 111 push the display out of range again. The shutter is pressed before the fruit is in the bucket in 311 of 399 Place Fruit and Photograph Logo episodes, water runs in 107 of 400 Scrub Bottle Then Fill Cup episodes although none finishes scrubbing, and the box lid moves before the pitcher lid in 340 of 400 Cover Pitcher and Box episodes. Nothing marks finished step, so completion must be inferred from the scene. 5.3.4. Task Grouping and Reliability Table 9 lists the grouping of Core-50 tasks by the hand skill that decides success, used in Figure 5a and throughout Section 5. Each task is assigned to exactly one group by its success condition; tasks that also require reaching and grasping are assigned to the later skill. The grouping is an analysis lens and is independent of the interaction and structure labels of the catalog. Twelve tasks selected by this ratio on even-indexed episodes reproduce 96% of the 28 pairwise orders measured on odd-indexed episodes (88% for random twelve-task subsets), and 24 tasks reproduce all of them. Episode-only 95% half-widths of the 50-task macro score are about 1.9, 1.3, and 0.9 points for 25, 50, and 100 episodes per task. Selecting checkpoint per task on half of the episodes and scoring it on the other half gives 32.9% versus 29.1% for the best single checkpoint. An earlier evaluation campaign of the same 𝜋0.5 and OpenWAM checkpoints used the fixed canonical prompt and single goal per task; on the 48 shared tasks it gives 24.8 versus 23.4% (𝜋0.5) and 30.5 versus 28.5% (OpenWAM), with per-task Spearman 𝜌 of 0.98 and 0.97 and per-task differences whose standard deviation (4.3 and 6.3 points) is close to the binomial expectation (5.1 and 5.5). All appearance factors and paraphrases are inside the training distribution, so these are invariance checks, not generalization results. 24 HandsOn: Generalizable Dexterous Manipulation Figure 10 Core-50 success (%) for eight trained multi-task checkpoints and GPT-6 (move_eef), grouped by hand skill  (Table 9)  . Trained cells have 100 episodes (99 for HY-Embodied on Place Wine Glass); GPT-6 cells have ten, so its 10-point increments reflect coarser sampling. DP, task IDs, and the same GPT-6 results are in Table 16. HandsOn: Generalizable Dexterous Manipulation 6. Discussion and Conclusion HandsOn provides common experimental basis for studying the scope and limits of manipulation competence. By treating embodiment, environment, and task structure as configurable experimental variables, it enables systematic investigation of how policy behavior changes across conditions and where generalization breaks down. Our trained-policy evaluation spans more than 40,000 Core-50 episodes and includes eight multi-task checkpoints, revealing substantial differences in performance across task categories. Pooled across those eight checkpoints, success rates reach 3551% for pushing, articulation, and pick-and-place, but remain at 23% for tool use and precision fitting. These disparities persist after accounting for demonstration count and expert demonstration duration. All tasks in both suites have been successfully demonstrated by human operators, making even the hardest cases concrete, achievable targets for policy improvement. prompted GPT-6 controller using move_eef succeeds in 29 of 660 trials: 5.2% on Core-50 and 1.9% on Transfer-16. Its saved action notes provide qualitative signs of task-aware sequencing and execution monitoring without benchmark demonstrations or finetuning, suggesting potential as high-level planner. Reliable execution remains difficult: the minimal harness requires the same model to translate subgoals into palm poses and up to 40 finger-joint targets with limited geometric and contact feedback. This motivates richer agent interfaces that connect high-level planning to state estimation and feedback-driven manipulation skills. The high dimensionality and contact sensitivity of dexterous tasks make this interface substantive design problem. Matched harness ablations are needed to quantify the contribution of these components. The diagnostic results point to common requirement: policies must regulate the state of an interaction throughout execution. They need to distinguish contacts that stabilize an object from those that actuate it, condition release on whether the partners hand has secured the object, and maintain achieved goals as the task progresses. Failures on composed tasks further highlight the importance of tracking completed steps and satisfying prerequisites before advancing. Together, these findings motivate learning methods that explicitly account for contact roles, inter-hand dependencies, and task progress. Future evaluations should measure both task completion and maintenance of success conditions, testing whether control improvements transfer across embodiments and to physical robots. Promising directions include evaluating VLM planners with richer agent harnesses, expanding embodiment and compositional-task coverage, strengthening paired simulation and real-world evaluation, and modeling contact state, inter-hand coordination, and task progress. 7. Future Work Tactile sensing. HandsOn policies receive vision and proprioception without tactile feedback, but the wrist cameras are mounted on the hand and the held object occludes them: once grasp forms, the very region the policy must control leaves the view. The failures we report sit exactly there. grasp that closes over button hides the button as it presses it; cut that loses handle contact happens on the far side of the object; goal pushed past its target is obscured by the hand doing the pushing. Tactile sensing would observe these contact events directly instead of inferring them from partially hidden view. Adding it requires taxels placed identically on the simulated and physical hand, contact model verified rather than assumed, and tasks that still admit visual solution, so that visual and tactile policies remain comparable on the same predicates. 26 HandsOn: Generalizable Dexterous Manipulation Quantified physical evaluation. The real-robot rollouts in Appendix show that simulation-trained checkpoints act sensibly on the physical platform, but they are recorded evidence, not measurement. physical success rate needs the discipline the simulated suite already has: paired simulation and real instances, an executable predicate on both, fixed trial count, and reported failure modes rather than selected successes. The protocol is specified in Appendix B.5; what remains is the trial budget to run it alongside simulation-plus-real and real-only training under an explicit data budget. Long-horizon household and production tasks. HandsOn scores individual skills, and even the compositional Transfer-16 tasks chain at most few operations. Household and production work is longer and less forgiving: tens of operations over changing world state, objects found rather than placed, and success measured in throughput and rework rather than binary predicate. Our failure analysis indicates what such suite must measure beyond success, namely whether policy tracks which steps are complete, notices that an earlier step went wrong, and can recover without restarting the episode. That requires long-horizon demonstrations, stage model that admits recovery rather than enforcing an ordered prefix, and evaluation that reports progress and interventions. Evaluating VLMs across richer agent harnesses. The GPT-6 experiment motivates evaluating VLMs with harnesses that add estimated object poses, contact feedback, reusable manipulation skills, and hierarchical control to direct move_eef commands. Comparing harnesses for fixed model, and models within shared harness, would help distinguish planning capability from interface design. Evaluations should match tasks, resets, physical-time and query budgets, disclose training of lower-level skills, and measure success, subgoal completion, recovery, and inference cost. This would establish when VLMs can serve as effective high-level planners for dexterous manipulation.

Interaction Type: = Primitive; = Functional; CR = Contact-rich. Task Structure: SS = Single-stage; RP = Repetitive; LH = Long-horizon (multi-stage). Asset Type: RB = Rigid body; AP = Articulated (prismatic); AR = Articulated (revolute); DF = Deformable. Classification notes. Primitive covers object transport or reorientation whose success is decided by reaching target configuration, including pushing, pulling, or rolling an object and moving an articulated part along its free degree of freedom (e.g., opening drawer or hinged lid). Functional requires the purposeful use of tool, appliance, or control interface (buttons, knobs, levers, faucets, triggers) to produce an effect. Contact-rich denotes tasks dominated by fine contact coordination, such as regrasping, precise mating, sustained contact-force regulation, coordinated bimanual articulation, or controlled deformation. RB describes each non-articulated rigid asset and does not limit task to one object. Rigid links of articulated assets are not counted separately. Deformable labels follow the current simulation model; visual liquid effects do not add DF label. In Task 08, the nail has prismatic joint relative to the wood block, and the hammer is separate rigid object. EVAL-Flex03 combines deformable foam pillow with rigid carton. SS denotes single semantic goal. RP denotes repeated applications of the same kind of manipulation operation, whereas LH requires distinct, dependent subgoals. Routine setup and terminal activation, release, or waiting do not by themselves turn repetitive task into LH. Task 39 (Set Timer) is classified as RP because its main manipulation consists of setting the minute and second values through button operations; starting the timer, withdrawing the hands, and observing countdown tick are terminal completion conditions. Qualitative Real-Robot Rollouts The videos released with this work show real-robot rollouts of checkpoints adapted using this datasets simulation demonstrations, without target-task real-robot demonstrations (Section 4.5); they are available at https://github.com/TsinghuaC3I/HandsOn. Two task families are shown: single-hand reach-and-place interactions and bimanual tasks that require both hands to hold their targets at once. We include these recordings as qualitative evidence that the simulated demonstrations transfer to physical dexterous hand: the policies establish contact with the intended object, carry it, and preserve the object pose through the hand transitions that the simulated episodes also rely on.
